Acropora.note: The fast-growing staghorn and table corals that build most of the framework of a modern reef.

Agnostus.note: A tiny, blind agnostid trilobite, a few millimetres long and so widespread that it zones Cambrian rocks across several continents.

Alvinella.note: The 'Pompeii worm', living on chimney walls in some of the hottest water any animal endures.

Ammolite.note: Not a taxon but a legacy: Bearpaw ammonite shells fossilised as the gem ammolite.

Ammonoidea.note: Coiled cephalopods diversifying fast; they will become the single best index fossil of the Mesozoic.

Amphipora.note: A rod-shaped stromatoporoid sponge that grew in dense thickets in the lagoons behind Devonian reefs.

Ampyx.note: A blind trilobite with three long spines, sometimes fossilised walking in single-file 'conga lines' across the sea floor.

Anomalocaris.note: A metre-long swimming predator with grasping appendages, and the first animal large enough to sit at the top of a food web.
Anomalocaris.hb: active nektonic swimmer with lateral flaps

Archaeocyatha.note: Sponge-grade cone-shaped reef builders that made the first animal reef framework and were extinct within twenty million years.

Asaphidae.note: Large, smooth-shelled trilobites, some with eyes on stalks, that dominate many Ordovician carbonate platforms.

Asaphus.note: A large asaphid trilobite of the Baltic Ordovician, some species carrying their eyes on long stalks to see over soft mud.

Australocoelia.note: Diagnostic of the cold high-latitude Gondwanan realm.

Australospirifer.note: A spiriferide brachiopod of the cold Malvinokaffric shelves of southern Gondwana.

Baculites.note: A straight-shelled ammonite so abundant it zones the entire seaway; the chalk records its coccolith plankton.

Bathymodiolus.note: Vent mussels living on sulphur-eating bacteria in their gills — no sunlight, no photosynthesis.

Belemnitida.note: Squid-like cephalopods whose bullet-shaped guards are among the commonest Jurassic fossils.

Bigotina.note: An early Cambrian trilobite of the West Gondwanan shelves, and the marker of the Bigotinid province.

Bivalvia.note: Clams, mussels, oysters and scallops. They take over the shallow sea floor from brachiopods after the end-Permian and never give it back.

Blastoidea.note: Bud-shaped echinoderms, abundant now and destined to disappear at the end of the Permian.

Brachiopoda.note: Shelled filter feeders that will dominate the shelf benthos for the next three hundred million years.

Bradgatia.note: A bush-shaped rangeomorph, its fronds radiating from a common base rather than standing on a stalk.

Bryozoa.note: Colonial encrusters and branching forms that build much of the reef and hardground framework.

Buchia.note: A small clam so abundant and fast-evolving it dates the whole boreal Jurassic-Cretaceous.

Burmeisteria.note: A homalonotid trilobite of the Malvinokaffric Realm, heavy-shelled and adapted to cold siliciclastic bottoms.

Calyptogena.note: Big white clams clustered in the warm sulphide flow around vents and seeps, fed by chemosynthetic bacteria in their gills.

Cameroceras.note: A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, possibly six metres long, hunting the shelf seas.
Cameroceras.hb: nektonic, with a long straight conical shell

Ceratites.note: The ammonite that dates the German Muschelkalk so precisely its zones are named after it.

Ceratitida.note: Ammonoids with frilled-saddle sutures, radiating from a handful of end-Permian survivors to become the standard timekeepers of the Triassic.

Charnia.note: Frond-shaped rangeomorphs anchored to the sea floor, feeding without a mouth or a gut.
Charnia.hb: sessile frond anchored by a holdfast, in the deep sea below the photic zone

Claraia.note: A thin-shelled bivalve that carpets post-extinction seafloors -- the classic disaster taxon.

Clarkeia.note: An index brachiopod of the cool Silurian Malvinokaffric seas, unlike anything in the tropics.

Cloudina.note: Stacked calcareous cones that built the first animal reefs, and carry the first drill holes made by a predator.
Cloudina.conf_note: Nama Group (Namibia) and correlative sections constrain Cloudina to ~550-539 Ma, ending at the Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary; the robust window is skewed old.

Congeria.note: An endemic brackish-water mussel that swarmed the isolated, freshening Paratethyan basins.

Crinoidea.note: Stalked echinoderms in meadows so dense that entire limestone formations are made of their debris.

Cucullaea.note: Robust ark clams, common on sandy sea floors from the Jurassic onward.

Cyprideis.note: A brackish ostracod that boomed as the Mediterranean's chemistry swung wildly during the salinity crisis.

Cyrtospirifer.note: A spiriferide brachiopod that spread almost worldwide in the Late Devonian, as the earlier provincial faunas merged.

Daonella.note: A flat, paper-thin bivalve of Triassic deep-shelf muds, often found in mass-mortality pavements.

Deltopecten.note: A scallop-like bivalve of the cool Permian shelves of Gondwana, found with glacial dropstones in the same beds.

Dickinsonia.note: A flat, segmented, centimetre-to-metre oval that left feeding traces as it moved; cholesterol in its tissues shows it was an animal.
Dickinsonia.dt: external digestion of the mat beneath it
Dickinsonia.hb: flat on a microbial mat, possibly mobile

Dreissena.note: 'Lago Mare' phase — brackish Paratethyan mussels flooding a Mediterranean nearly emptied and freshened before the Atlantic broke back in.

Encrinus.note: Meadows of stalked crinoids ('sea lilies') whose disarticulated ossicles make crinoidal limestone.

Endemic molluscs.note: Cut off from the world ocean, the sea evolved its own peculiar low-salinity mollusc faunas.

Endoceras.note: A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, metres long, hunting the Ordovician carbonate platform.

Eoredlichia.note: An early redlichiid trilobite of South China, found in the Chengjiang Lagerstaette alongside soft-bodied animals.

Ernietta.note: Partly buried, sack-like, in shifting sand
Ernietta.hb: partly buried, sack-like, in shifting sand

Euphausiacea.note: Krill: swarming shrimp-like crustaceans. In the Southern Ocean they are the single link between diatoms and everything larger -- whales, seals, penguins and fish all feed on them.

Eurydesma.note: A thick-shelled cold-water bivalve of the peri-glacial Gondwanan seas.
Eurydesma.hb: cold-water shelf, often in glacial dropstone facies

Euryhaline molluscs.note: After the Messinian salinity crisis dried the basin, salt-tolerant survivors and Atlantic recolonisers rebuild the fauna.

Eurypterida.note: Sea scorpions, in decline for a hundred million years, finally gone.

Eurypterus.note: Sea scorpions patrolling brackish lagoons, some large enough to take vertebrate prey.

Fenestrata.note: Lacy, net-like bryozoans that built small reefs and meadows on Palaeozoic carbonate shelves.

Fractofusus.note: Shows evidence of reproduction by stolons.
Fractofusus.hb: reclining on the sea floor, deep water

Goniatitida.note: Palaeozoic ammonoids with zigzag sutures, abundant in the open water above Devonian to Permian shelves and basins.

Graptolithina.note: Colonial hemichordates drifting in open water, whose fast turnover makes them the timekeepers of the Ordovician.
Graptolithina.conf_note: The branching graptolite rhabdosome (Graptoloidea+Dendroidea) dies out by the end-Mississippian; only the unrelated-looking crown pterobranchs survive, so the drawable form is not extant.

Gryphaea.note: 'Devil's toenails' — thick curved oysters strewn across the Jurassic seabed of western North America.

Hallucigenia.note: A spined, stilt-legged lobopodian reconstructed upside-down and backwards for decades before anyone got it right.

Halobia.note: A thin flat 'paper clam' blanketing deep Tethyan Triassic seafloors along the drifting blocks.

Halysites.note: Chain coral, a diagnostic Silurian reef builder whose colonies form linked palisades.

Hexactinellida.note: Glass sponges building a reef belt along the Tethyan shelf larger than any reef system before or since.

Hippurites.note: A rudist bivalve grown into a tall cone with a lid, packed upright in thickets that built the reefs of the Late Cretaceous Tethys in place of corals.

Hirnantia.note: The name-bearer of the cold-water brachiopod fauna that briefly took over the world's shelves during the glaciation.
Hirnantia.conf_note: Hirnantia is tied tightly to the Hirnantian Stage/glaciation (445.2-443.8 Ma); the robust PBDB window is broader than the genus's true stratigraphic tie.

Holmia.note: An olenellid trilobite of the early Cambrian Baltic and Laurentian shelves.

Inoceramidae.note: Big flat clams littering Cretaceous seafloors, sometimes shells over a metre across.

Inoceramus.note: A thick-shelled bivalve of Cretaceous shelf muds, some species reaching a metre across, and often the only large fossil in an otherwise barren chalk.

Kimberella.note: A bilaterally symmetrical grazer that scraped mats with a feeding structure -- the best candidate for an early mollusc relative.

Kjerulfia.note: A large olenellid trilobite of the early Cambrian Scandinavian shelf.

Lingula.note: A burrowing brachiopod that survives everything and looks much the same today.

Malvinokaffric brachiopods.note: A distinctive low-diversity cold-water shelly province across South America, South Africa and the Falklands.

Megalodontidae.note: Thick heart-shaped bivalves crowding the Triassic Tethyan carbonate platforms.

Megistaspis.note: A big asaphid trilobite of the Baltoscandian Ordovician, common in the orthoceratite limestones.

Mesolimulus.note: A horseshoe crab preserved at the end of its own death-track across the anoxic mud.

Monograptus.note: Single-row graptolites that swarm Silurian seas, evolving so fast that they date the rocks they drift into.

Mucrospirifer.note: A winged spiriferide brachiopod of the Middle Devonian Appalachian seas, its hinge drawn out into long points.

Mytilus.note: The blue mussel, a Pacific native that crossed into the Atlantic when the Bering Strait opened.

Namacalathus.note: A goblet-shaped skeletal organism from the Nama Group, part of the first mineralised reef community.
Namacalathus.conf_note: Known only from the terminal Ediacaran Nama-type reef assemblage, ~550-539 Ma, matching Cloudina; not a hyolith (no conical shell).

Nautiloidea.note: Coiled cephalopods that radiated after the Permian extinction and still cruise Indo-Pacific reef slopes today as Nautilus.
Nautiloidea.conf_note: form=nautilus (coiled Nautilida) is Triassic-Recent (~247-0 Ma); Early Palaeozoic straight-shelled nautiloids are covered separately by orthocone genera like Cameroceras.

Nautilus.note: The living Nautilus, a survivor of the once-vast shelled-cephalopod dynasties, still haunts these depths.

Neseuretus.note: A calymenid trilobite of the cold, muddy shelves that ringed high-latitude Gondwana.

Olenellus.note: A spiny olenellid trilobite that defines the Laurentian faunal province of the Cambrian tropics.

Orthida.note: The earliest articulate brachiopods, ribbed and nearly symmetrical, abundant on Ordovician shelves.

Ostracoda.note: Tiny bivalved crustaceans that become one of the most continuous fossil records of the entire Phanerozoic.

Otoceras.note: The ammonoid whose first appearance defines the base of the Triassic.

Paradoxides.note: A large spiny trilobite of the Baltic-Avalonian 'Atlantic' province, unknown on Cambrian Laurentia.

Pebasian molluscs.note: An endemic radiation of hundreds of snail and mussel species, found nowhere else, whose shells date the wetland bed by bed.

Pentacrinites.note: Stalked crinoids that rafted on driftwood over the open sea.

Pentamerus.note: A large Silurian brachiopod that formed dense shell banks across carbonate shelves.

Placenticeras.note: A large disc-shaped ammonite, some shells punctured by mosasaur tooth-marks.

Porifera.note: Sponges. Molecular clocks and disputed biomarkers place their origin in the Tonian or Cryogenian; unambiguous body fossils come later.

Porites.note: A massive, slow-growing reef coral whose skeleton records annual bands like tree rings.

Posidonia.note: A thin-shelled bivalve that paves the black, oxygen-poor shales of Jurassic Europe -- the 'Posidonia Shale' -- by the million.

Productida.note: Spiny, thick-shelled brachiopods resting on soft carbonate mud, the dominant shellfish of the late Paleozoic sea floor.

Pteridinium.note: A quilted, vane-like Ediacaran organism of the terminal-Ediacaran Nama sandflats.

Pterygotus.note: A giant eurypterid with grasping claws, one of the largest arthropods that ever lived.
Pterygotus.hb: nektonic sea scorpion with crushing chelicerae

Rangea.note: A fractal frondose Ediacaran of the Namibian shelf, type of the whole rangeomorph group.

Rangeomorpha.note: Fractal, self-similar fronds anchored in deep water at Mistaken Point -- a body plan with no modern counterpart.

Redlichia.note: A large, spiny redlichiid trilobite that typifies the Cambrian shelves of Gondwana and China.

Riftia.note: Giant tube worms up to 2 m long, mouthless and gutless, fed by symbiotic bacteria — icons of the 1977 vent discovery.

Rimicaris.note: Swarming eyeless vent shrimp that crowd Atlantic and Indian Ocean chimneys, farming bacteria on their shells.

Rugosa.note: Solitary and colonial Palaeozoic corals, extinguished entirely; the corals that follow are a different lineage.

Schmidtiellus.note: One of the oldest trilobites of Baltica, from the earliest Cambrian shelly faunas.

Scleractinia.note: Stone corals appear from nowhere and rebuild the reef ecosystem the Permian destroyed; every modern reef descends from them.

Spriggina.note: A segmented Ediacaran form with a shield-like head end, argued over for decades as a possible early arthropod relative.

Stringocephalus.note: A Middle Devonian index fossil of the Old World Realm.

Stromatoporoidea.note: Calcified sponges that are the principal reef framework builders of the Middle Palaeozoic.

Tabulata.note: Colonial corals with honeycomb skeletons, joining stromatoporoids as reef builders.

Tribrachidium.note: A body plan with no counterpart in any living phylum.

Tridacna.note: The giant clam: up to 1.3 m and 250 kg, fixed for life on an Indo-Pacific reef and fed largely by the algae it farms in its own mantle.

Trilobita.note: The defining Cambrian arthropod: armoured, mobile, with compound eyes made of calcite crystals.
Trilobita.conf_note: Unambiguous mineralised trilobites first appear in Cambrian Stage 3 (~521 Ma); 538.8 Ma is the base-Cambrian bin edge, not the true FAD.

Tropidoleptus.note: A brachiopod that marks the Devonian seas of the Americas, from the Appalachian basin to the cool southern shelves.

Waagenophyllidae.note: Permian rugose corals of the rich Tethyan reefs as the ocean starts to close behind Cimmeria.

Waagenophyllum.note: A rugose coral of Permian Tethyan reefs, colonial and thickly walled.

Wiwaxia.note: A scale-covered mat grazer whose affinities have been argued between molluscs and annelids for a century.
Wiwaxia.hb: benthic, armoured with sclerites and spines

Yorgia.note: Found with a trail of its own feeding impressions.

calymenid trilobites.note: Robust, strongly enrolling trilobites that dominate the cold high-latitude Ordovician shelves where reefs are absent.

ceratitid ammonoids.note: The ammonoid group that radiated through the Triassic from the handful of lineages that survived the end-Permian bottleneck.

giant clams.note: Tridacna and its relatives, which farm symbiotic algae inside their own mantle tissue on shallow tropical reefs.

hyoliths.note: Small conical Cambrian shells with a lid and a pair of props. What they actually were was argued for 175 years -- probably relatives of brachiopods.

orthoceratid nautiloids.note: Straight-shelled cephalopods whose conchs pave the Baltic orthoceratite limestone -- the rock takes its name from them.

rudists.note: They displace corals as the main tropical reef builder for much of the Cretaceous, and die at the K-Pg.

stromatoporoids.note: Calcified sponges that built the reefs of the Ordovician through Devonian, in the long gap between the archaeocyaths and the modern corals.

tabulate corals.note: Colonial corals built from stacked tubes with floors across them. Palaeozoic reef framework, extinct at the end-Permian.
